problem.title: Erdos 663: the least prime missing from k consecutive integers, for every k
problem.informal_statement:
Let q(n,k) be the least prime that does not divide the product of (n+i) for 1 <= i <= k. Prove that for every integer k >= 2 and every rational epsilon > 0 there is a positive integer N, permitted to depend on both k and epsilon, such that q(n,k) < (1 + epsilon) * log n for every integer n > N, where log is the natural logarithm.

The target is not narrowed to one k. The asymptotic is written in explicit epsilon-N form so the quantifier order is auditable: k and epsilon both come before N, and N may depend on both. The first bounded slice is narrower on purpose: it works at the waypoint value k = 3 and reproduces the easy bound whose constant is k. That waypoint is a step on the route, never a substitute for the target, and it establishes nothing about any other k or about how N behaves as k varies.

target_claim.statement: For every integer k >= 2 and every rational epsilon > 0 there exists a positive integer N, permitted to depend on both k and epsilon, such that for every integer n > N, q(n,k) < (1 + epsilon) * log n, where q(n,k) is the least prime p that does not divide the product of (n+i) for 1 <= i <= k and log is the natural logarithm.

assumption_claims.statement: For an integer k >= 2 and a positive integer n, q(n,k) is the least prime p such that p does not divide the product of (n+i) over 1 <= i <= k. The product is over i from 1 to k inclusive, so it is (n+1)...(n+k) and starts at n+1, not at n. The product is a positive integer greater than 1 with finitely many prime divisors, so q(n,k) exists and is unique.

k = 3 is NOT a hypothesis of the target claim. It is the waypoint value of the bounded first slice: the target statement restricted to the single value k = 3. Three reasons make 3 the right first k. It is the least k for which the forced divisor set is exactly {2,3}, so the first prime whose divisibility is a genuine residue condition is 5. The per-prime residue condition covers 3 of p classes, which is small enough for an extremal search to reach informative P inside a bounded envelope and large enough that extremal n are not astronomically sparse. And k = 2 is a materially easier and structurally different configuration, with forced divisor set {2} and only 2 of p classes per prime. The waypoint is a step on the route to the target and never a substitute for it.

n ranges over the positive integers from 1 upward. Zero and negative n are outside the statement. Since log 1 = 0 and log 2 is below 0.7 while q(n,k) is always a prime greater than k, small n are genuine false instances of the inequality and are absorbed by the threshold N rather than treated as counterexamples.
log denotes the natural logarithm, base e. A base-2 or base-10 reading multiplies the right-hand side by a constant and is a different claim; both are rejected readings.

epsilon is quantified over the positive rationals rather than the positive reals. The two statements are equivalent because the inequality is monotone increasing in epsilon and the positive rationals are dense in the positive reals: any real epsilon > 0 is bounded below by a positive rational. Rational epsilon is chosen so that every threshold computation stays inside exact rational arithmetic.

For every k >= 2 and every n >= 1, any block of k consecutive integers contains a multiple of every prime p <= k, because it contains p consecutive integers. Hence every prime at most k divides (n+1)...(n+k), and q(n,k) is a prime strictly greater than k. At the waypoint value k = 3 this says 2 and 3 always divide (n+1)(n+2)(n+3), so q(n,3) >= 5.

For a prime p > k, p divides (n+1)...(n+k) if and only if n mod p lies in the set {p-1, p-2, ..., p-k}, and those k residues are distinct. Consequently q(n,k) > P holds if and only if n satisfies one of exactly k residue conditions modulo each prime p with k < p <= P, and by the Chinese remainder theorem the set of such n is a union of residue classes modulo the product of those primes.

The Chebyshev function theta(x) = sum of log p over primes p <= x satisfies theta(x) = x + o(x) as x -> infinity, and elementary explicit bounds of the form theta(x) > c*x hold for all x >= 2 with an explicit constant c. This is a textbook fact; any explicit constant actually used must be cited to an acquired source or re-derived, not assumed at the value a model recalls.

The easy upper bound q(n,k) <= (1 + o(1)) * k * log n follows because every prime below q(n,k) divides (n+1)...(n+k), so theta(q(n,k)) - log q(n,k) <= log((n+1)...(n+k)) <= k*log(n+k), and theta(x) = x + o(x) then bounds q(n,k). This route must be re-derived inside the slice with explicit constants and an explicit threshold as a function of k and epsilon. It is recorded as the route, not assumed as a result. The constant it produces is k, and the target constant is 1, so the factor-k gap is the reported open obligation; at the waypoint k = 3 it is the factor-3 gap.

The planning dossier reports Erdos Problem 663 as a catalogue entry asking whether q(n,k) < (1 + o(1)) log n for every fixed k, and reports the (1 + o(1)) k log n bound as easy. This is the load-bearing untrusted claim: the frozen target is that question for every k, and nothing here has been acquired, quoted from a primary source, or reviewed. Nothing in this package asserts that the target is open, novel, or unproved. It must be covered by the ADR-0055 pre-research novelty re-check before work starts.

Whether the original source states the product as (n+1)...(n+k) or as n(n+1)...(n+k-1), and whether it permits the threshold to depend on k or intends a threshold uniform in k, is not verifiable offline. The frozen reading is the product from n+1 to n+k with N permitted to depend on k. A different indexing shifts n by one, and a k-independent N is a strictly stronger statement; both are rejected readings recorded for audit.

All integer work is exact: products, factorizations, residues, and Chinese remainder reconstructions use arbitrary-precision integers. Comparisons against log n are performed with rational interval enclosures of log n whose endpoints are rationals from a truncated series with a certified remainder bound, used only to exclude, never to conclude equality. Floating-point ratios such as q(n,k) / log n may be printed as exploration-only guidance and may never enter a certificate.

No computation over a finite range of n can establish the asymptotic claim, and no finite range can refute it either, because the claim only constrains n beyond an unspecified threshold. A finite sweep can produce certified extremal n, a certified lower bound on the supremum over the swept range of q(n,k) / log n, and structural characterizations of long initial-prime coverage. It can never be promoted to the limit statement in either direction.

The target quantifies over every integer k >= 2, so the behaviour of the threshold in k is part of what must be established and is not a caveat. N is permitted to depend on k and must be: because q(n,k) > k always, every admissible N satisfies N >= exp(k/(1+epsilon)), an exact necessary lower bound derived from small_primes_always_divide. Every threshold, error term, and implied constant produced by work on this target must therefore be written as an explicit function of k and epsilon. An unquantified o(1), an unnamed implied constant, or a threshold that silently absorbs a k-dependence is not admissible output, and work at the single value k = 3 establishes nothing about any other k.

formalization.statement: forall k in Z with k >= 2, forall epsilon in Q with epsilon > 0, exists N in Z with N >= 1 and N depending on k and epsilon, forall n in Z with n > N, q(n,k) < (1 + epsilon) * log(n), where q(n,k) = min { p : p prime and p does not divide the product of (n+i) for 1 <= i <= k } and log is the natural logarithm
quantifiers: forall k an integer with k >= 2
exists N a positive integer, permitted to depend on both k and epsilon
forall n an integer with n > N

quantifier_mapping: forall k an integer with k >= 2; every k is in scope and none is fixed
forall epsilon in Q with epsilon > 0, exists N, forall integers n > N
q(n,k) < (1 + epsilon) * log n with k and epsilon both quantified before N and N permitted to depend on both
n an integer with n > N; the underlying range is the positive integers from 1
the value k = 3 of the first slice
not a quantifier of the target; it scopes only the waypoint proved en route
definition_mapping: the least prime not dividing the product of (n+i) for 1 <= i <= k
(n+1)...(n+k); the product starts at n+1, not at n
natural logarithm of n, base e
long initial-prime coverage of k consecutive integers
the property that every prime at most P divides (n+1)...(n+k), which is exactly the condition q(n,k) > P
an n that attains the maximum of q(n,k) over a stated finite range, or the least n with q(n,k) > P for a stated P and k
a strictly weaker statement proved en route to the target, recorded as progress and never as the target
assumption_delta: The frozen target adds no hypothesis to the planning dossier's candidate statement: it quantifies over every integer k >= 2 and every rational epsilon > 0, with no k fixed.
The implicit (1 + o(1)) is replaced by the explicit epsilon-N form with k and epsilon both quantified before N; this is the same statement written so the quantifier order cannot drift.

N is permitted to depend on both k and epsilon, and must be: the target asserts the conclusion for each k, not a single threshold serving every k at once. A k-independent N is a strictly stronger statement and is a rejected reading.

epsilon is quantified over positive rationals rather than positive reals; the statements are equivalent by monotonicity in epsilon and density of the rationals, and the rational choice keeps threshold computations exact.
The logarithm base is pinned to e; no published constant is assumed, including the explicit Chebyshev constant used in any re-derivation.

The value k = 3 is not part of the target. It scopes the first slice's waypoint only, and the slice's k = 3 work establishes nothing about any other k and nothing about how N and the error terms behave as k varies, which is exactly what the target's quantification over k requires.
edge_case_delta: For every k >= 2 and n >= 1, every prime at most k divides the product, so q(n,k) is a prime strictly greater than k; at the waypoint value k = 3 this gives q(n,3) >= 5.
Small n are genuine false instances: log n is at most 0.7 for n <= 2 while q(n,k) > k >= 2, so they are absorbed by the threshold N and are not counterexamples to the frozen claim.
n ranges over positive integers only; the statement says nothing about n <= 0, where the product can vanish and q would be undefined.

The inequality is strict, and the right-hand side is irrational for every n >= 2 and rational epsilon, so the boundary case of equality does not arise; the frozen statement does not rely on that observation.

Because q(n,k) > k always, every admissible N satisfies N >= exp(k/(1+epsilon)): the threshold provably grows at least exponentially in k, so the k-dependence of N is load-bearing rather than incidental.

success_criteria: an exact re-derivation of the easy upper bound with an explicit threshold N as a function of k and epsilon and explicit constants, every step replayable in exact rational arithmetic, recorded as progress toward the target and never as the target because the constant it yields is k and not 1

the waypoint proved, namely the target statement at the single value k = 3 with an explicit threshold N as a function of epsilon, recorded as progress toward the target and never as the target, since the target quantifies over every integer k >= 2

an exactly certified extremal n at the waypoint value k = 3, together with the complete list of primes dividing (n+1)(n+2)(n+3) and a rational enclosure of log n that pins the ratio q(n,3) / log n at that n

or, and this is the realistic outcome for a first slice against a full open case, an explicit unresolved outcome recording the smallest remaining obligation: the re-derived constant written as an explicit function of k, the gap between it and the target constant 1, and the fact that nothing has been established about how the threshold behaves as k varies
stopping_rules: stop when the easy upper bound is re-derived with explicit constants and an explicit threshold as a function of k and epsilon
stop when an exact certificate establishes a new largest certified value of q(n,3) / log n inside the frozen waypoint search envelope
stop when the fresh model spend reaches USD 20
stop when no derivation obligation has been closed and no new extremal n has been certified for two consecutive review points
never promote a finite sweep of n into the asymptotic claim or into its refutation: exhausting any range of n leaves the limit untouched
never present the k = 3 waypoint as the target: the target quantifies over every integer k >= 2, and one value of k establishes nothing about the others or about the behaviour of the threshold in k
